rules.statement: In production service code, don't keep state that matters beyond a single request in process memory; put durable state in the database and shared ephemeral state behind a shared-state abstraction backed by a distributed store, so any replica can serve any request.
rules.why: Services run as interchangeable, disposable replicas with no sticky sessions; state held in one process is lost when that replica is replaced and is invisible to the other replicas.
rules.check: Look for static or singleton dictionaries, caches, queues or in-process job stores holding data that other requests or replicas depend on, and for designs that need session affinity.

rules.statement: Don't add a feature that relies on sticky sessions or request affinity to a specific replica.
rules.why: Any replica must serve any request, so a feature that only works when follow-up requests reach the same instance breaks behind a load balancer.
rules.check: Look for per-user or per-flow data cached locally and read back on a later request, or configuration enabling session affinity.

rules.statement: Outbound calls to other services use an explicit timeout and bounded retries with jitter, never unbounded or fixed-interval retry loops.
rules.why: The service must stay available when a dependency fails; without timeouts and with unbounded or synchronized retries, a failure spreads and turns into a retry storm.
rules.check: Look for HttpClient or other remote calls without a timeout, retry loops with no maximum attempt count, and retry delays with no random jitter.

rules.statement: Read service configuration from the environment and the configuration system, and send logs to stdout rather than to local files.
rules.why: Following twelve-factor operation lets the same immutable artifact run in every environment, and containers run with read-only root filesystems.
rules.check: Look for hard-coded per-environment values, configuration or log files written to the local filesystem, and file log sinks.

rules.statement: In production service code, don't write to the container's local filesystem at runtime outside an explicitly mounted writable volume or temporary directory.
rules.why: Containers run with read-only root filesystems, and a change ships as a new release, never as an edit in place.
rules.check: Look for File/Directory writes to paths under the app directory or other fixed paths, and for code that changes deployed files at runtime.

rules.statement: Make services start fast and shut down gracefully: honor the host's stopping token, and let in-flight work finish or hand it off durably.
rules.why: Replicas are replaced routinely during rollouts and node churn, so slow starts or abrupt shutdowns lose work and hurt availability.
rules.check: Look for background services that ignore the CancellationToken or IHostApplicationLifetime stopping signal, long blocking startup work, and in-process work that is lost on shutdown.

rules.statement: Write database schema changes as expand-then-contract migrations, so the previous release keeps working against the new schema.
rules.why: Rollouts are progressive, so the old and new releases run side by side against the same database.
rules.check: Look for migrations that drop, rename or retype columns or tables, or add NOT NULL columns without defaults, while the currently deployed code still uses them.

rules.statement: Never commit secrets or long-lived credentials to Git; use OIDC or workload identity, or a secret store or KMS.
rules.why: The platform is secure by default: least privilege, no secrets in Git, and no long-lived credentials.
rules.check: Look for keys, passwords, connection strings with credentials, or access tokens in source, config, workflow or infrastructure files.

rules.statement: Emit metrics, logs and traces through OpenTelemetry instead of vendor-specific telemetry SDKs.
rules.why: The platform must be observable and portable through open standards, so a vendor can be swapped by replacing one component.
rules.check: Look for direct dependencies on vendor-specific telemetry or APM client libraries in place of OpenTelemetry APIs such as ActivitySource, Meter and ILogger exporters.
